:::{#thm-eigenvalue-singular}
#### Eigenvalues are where $\matr{A} - \eigval \matr{I}$ is singular

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ matrix and $\eigval$ a real number.
Then $\eigval$ is an eigenvalue of $\matr{A}$ (@def-eigenvalue)
exactly when $\matr{A} - \eigval\,\matr{I}_p$ is singular (@def-invertible-matrix).
In particular, $\matr{A}$ is singular exactly when $0$ is one of its eigenvalues;
and each eigenspace $\mathcal{E}_\eigval$ (@def-eigenspace) is a subspace of $\reals^p$
consisting of $\vzero$ and the eigenvectors for $\eigval$.

:::

::: proof

For any $\vecf{v} \in \reals^p$,

$$
\ba
(\matr{A} - \eigval\,\matr{I}_p)\,\vecf{v}
&= \matr{A} \vecf{v} - (\eigval\,\matr{I}_p)\,\vecf{v}
&& \text{(@thm-scalar-matmul, the difference law)}
\\
&= \matr{A} \vecf{v} - \eigval\,(\matr{I}_p \vecf{v})
&& \text{(@thm-scalar-matmul, the scalar factor)}
\\
&= \matr{A} \vecf{v} - \eigval \vecf{v},
&& \text{(@thm-identity)}
\ea
$$

so $\matr{A} \vecf{v} = \eigval \vecf{v}$ exactly when $\vecf{v} \in \mathcal{N}(\matr{A} - \eigval\,\matr{I}_p)$;
the nonzero such $\vecf{v}$ are the eigenvectors for $\eigval$.
So $\eigval$ is an eigenvalue exactly when that null space contains a nonzero vector,
which by @thm-invertible-rank is exactly when $\matr{A} - \eigval\,\matr{I}_p$ is singular.
With $\eigval = 0$, $\matr{A} - 0\,\matr{I}_p = \matr{A}$.
An eigenspace is a null space, so it is a subspace (@thm-null-space-subspace).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-eigenvalue-singular}
#### Eigenvalues and singular matrices

For $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$,
$\matr{A} - 3\,\matr{I}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ is singular
(its columns are negatives of each other, so its rank is $1$),
matching the eigenvalue $3$ of @exm-eigenvalue.
$\matr{A}$ itself has rank $2$, since $c_1 (2, 1) + c_2 (1, 2) = (2c_1 + c_2, c_1 + 2c_2)$
is $\vzero$ only if $c_1 = c_2 = 0$ (subtract twice the second entry from the first: $-3c_2 = 0$, and then the second entry gives $c_1 = 0$);
so it is invertible (@thm-invertible-rank),
and $0$ is not an eigenvalue.
The singular matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalue $0$,
with eigenvector $(1, -1)$.

:::
